summary:
MARSWARD is a hands‑on platform that lets astronauts and mission planners look at ground and choose safer paths on Mars. MARSWARD was built with Python, Flask, JavaScript and OpenLayers. MARSWARD pulls NASA’s Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) elevation data to show the surface examine slopes, spot possible dangers and create best routes, with the A* pathfinding algorithm.

By mixing NASA terrain data with route choices that know the ground MARSWARD shows users how hard it is to walk across Mars. MARSWARD’s future Survival Simulator and Science Explorer will help with planning supplies. Doing science.

MARSWARD tackles the problem of living and working on planets by turning tough planetary data into a simple interactive guide. MARSWARD is vital because good ground checks, clear routes and knowing what supplies are needed cut risk and help human trips to Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works

MARSWARD is a mission-planning console for Jezero Crater on Mars. It takes real NASA elevation data and answers one question: can this crew make this trip safely? You click a start and a destination (or pick one of six named science stops), choose a crew rover or an astronaut on foot, and set the conditions: speed, time limit, time at the destination, reserve, slope limit, dust opacity and air temperature. The app then calculates a route and returns a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict with the reasons behind it.

Under the hood, the server turns NASA MOLA elevation into slope for every map square and sorts each square into four hazard classes: Gentle (0–5°), Moderate (5–15°), Steep (15–25°) and Very Steep (over 25°). An A* search then finds a route that never crosses squares above the slope limit (20° by default). Travel time is slower on slopes, and the planner adds time at the destination and compares the total with the time limit. It also checks the steepest slope, dust and air temperature. A Survival Simulator checks whether water, food and oxygen last the mission for a given crew, with an emergency reserve. A Science Explorer adds facts about Mars, Jezero and the dataset, plus Perseverance surface conditions.

Benefits

  • Gives a clear, explainable decision (GO / CAUTION / NO-GO) instead of raw terrain data.
  • Shows why a trip fails, so planners can change the destination, speed, time limit or slope limit and recalculate.
  • Needs no setup. It runs in a browser, and the Jezero elevation data is bundled.

Intended impact

The goal is to make planetary terrain data usable by people who aren’t GIS experts: students, educators and mission-concept planners. It’s planning support for research and education, not an operational safety guarantee, and the app says so.

Tools and technologies

Python, Flask, NumPy and NetworkX on the server. JavaScript, HTML and CSS on the front end, with OpenLayers for the map. The data is NASA MOLA MEGDR elevation (Mars Global Surveyor), NASA Mars Trek base maps (MOLA shaded relief and Viking colour), Perseverance MEDA weather data, the IAU Gazetteer (USGS) for place names, and NASA/TP-2015-218570 for life-support values. The site is hosted on Vercel. No special hardware is needed, just a web browser.

Creativity

  • The verdict engine combines terrain, travel time, dust and temperature in one result.
  • Travel time uses the shape of Tobler’s hiking function, so steep ground slows the route.
  • A “blocked terrain” view shows exactly which squares the planner refuses to cross.
  • A mission-control interface lets you watch the chosen explorer drive the route from a top view, a side view with an elevation profile, or a driver chase cam.

Factors we considered

  • Data resolution: each elevation pixel is about 926 m, so slopes are regional averages and boulders, scarps and sand aren’t visible.
  • Editable limits: slope limit, time limit, cold threshold and speeds are planning assumptions, and the dust thresholds are our own choice based on levels Perseverance measured.
  • User-entered conditions: dust and temperature are entered by the user rather than loaded from a live feed.
  • Source quality: survival rates come from secondary sources, and two science stop positions are approximate.
  • Transparency: every limitation is stated in the app and the README.
